title: Chemical equilibrium: direction, extent and what remains
attribution: Original course, numerical cases and explanations by HAMON estate contributor776fc776b752. Background: IUPAC Gold Book, equilibrium constant(E02177), standard equilibrium constant(S05915) and chemical equilibrium(C01023); https://goldbook.iupac.org/terms/view/E02177 ; https://goldbook.iupac.org/terms/view/S05915 ; https://goldbook.iupac.org/terms/view/C01023 . MIT OpenCourseWare3.091, Fall2018, extra notes on equilibrium(Lecture28): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-091-introduction-to-solid-state-chemistry-fall-2018/0de26165d2c924f4a46e7cb1e3118c23_MIT3_091F18_Equilibrium.pdf . The worked model is one ideal homogeneous A+B⇌C reaction at fixed temperature and volume, with activity coefficients set to1 and c°=1mol L−1. It does not predict substance-specific behavior or reaction rates.
license: Original course wording and numerical cases: CC0-1.0. Referenced works retain their own terms. No textbook passages, figures or exercises are reproduced.

items.prompt: For ideal A + B ⇌ C, use the dimensionless concentration ratios a=[A]/c°, b=[B]/c° and c=[C]/c°. A mixture has a=2, b=3 and c=3. What is its instantaneous reaction quotient Q=c/(ab)?
items.explanation: The denominator is 2×3=6, so Q=3/6=1/2. Each concentration was divided by the same declared standard concentration before forming the activity quotient; Q is dimensionless.
items.transfer: Keep a=2 and b=3, but change c to6. Find Q and explain why it changes even though the reaction formula does not.

items.prompt: For the fixed-temperature ideal reaction A + B ⇌ C, a mixture has Q=1/2 and the supplied equilibrium constant is K=2. Which net composition change moves it toward equilibrium?
options: A and B decrease while C increases.
A and B increase while C decreases.
All three must already be at equilibrium.
The mixture must change K to1/2.
items.explanation: Q<K, so the forward change is favored in this ideal model. Consuming A and B while forming C raises c/(ab). K is held fixed for the declared reaction and temperature; the calculation does not specify how quickly composition changes.
items.transfer: For the same K=2, predict the direction if a different mixture has Q=4. State what the quotient comparison does not tell you about time.

items.prompt: A reversible reaction is at chemical equilibrium in a closed system with constant conditions. Which statement correctly describes this state?
options: Every reactant concentration equals every product concentration.
Every reactant has been completely consumed.
The forward reaction has stopped and only the reverse reaction continues.
Forward and reverse rates balance, so there is no net composition change.
items.explanation: Equilibrium is dynamic: balanced forward and reverse rates give a steady composition. Equal rates do not require equal concentrations, and they do not require either direction to stop.
items.transfer: If observed concentrations stay constant, why does that observation alone not establish the numerical values of the two reaction rates?

items.prompt: For ideal A + B ⇌ C, initial normalized concentrations are a=3, b=2 and c=1. A signed forward extent of x=1/2 gives (a−x,b−x,c+x). Which resulting triple is correct?
items.explanation: A and B each decrease by1/2, while C increases by1/2: (3−1/2,2−1/2,1+1/2)=(5/2,3/2,3/2). This is a feasible composition; calling it equilibrium would also require checking K.
items.transfer: Use x=−1/2 with the same initial mixture. Find all three concentrations and name the net direction.

items.prompt: For ideal A + B ⇌ C with initial a=3, b=2 and c=1, a signed extent x produces (3−x,2−x,1+x). Which complete interval keeps every concentration nonnegative?
items.explanation: C≥0 requires x≥−1. A≥0 requires x≤3, and B≥0 requires x≤2. Combining all three gives −1≤x≤2. The negative part permits reverse conversion of C.
items.transfer: For a=1, b=4 and c=2, derive the complete feasible interval. Identify the species that reaches zero at each endpoint.

items.prompt: In a closed fixed-volume A + B ⇌ C model, concentrations change by (−x,−x,+x). Which two sums stay unchanged for every feasible x?
options: a+b and a+b+c
a+c and b+c
a alone and b alone
a+b+c and c alone
items.explanation: (a−x)+(c+x)=a+c, and likewise b+c is constant. These are the two component totals for this stoichiometry. The sum a+b+c changes by−x, so it is not a conserved count of molecules.
items.transfer: For initial (a,b,c)=(3,2,1), compute both conserved totals and verify them at x=−1/2.

items.prompt: For ideal A + B ⇌ C, initial normalized concentrations are (a,b,c)=(2,2,0), and K=1. Which triple both preserves the component totals and satisfies Q=c/(ab)=1?
items.explanation: The triple(1,1,1) has a+c=b+c=2 and Q=1/(1×1)=1. It corresponds to x=1. Complete conversion to(0,0,2) has no finite quotient and is not the equilibrium composition for this positive finite K.
items.transfer: Start instead from(0,0,2) with K=1. Give the signed extent leading to the same equilibrium triple and explain why the component totals match.

items.prompt: For ideal A + B ⇌ C, start from normalized concentrations(0,0,2) with K=1. Which statement treats the zero reactant concentrations correctly?
options: Q=0, so only forward conversion is possible.
No conversion is possible because both reactants start at zero.
The initial quotient is undefined, but reverse conversion can create A and B.
An undefined quotient proves the mixture is already at equilibrium.
items.explanation: Q=c/(ab) would divide2 by0, so it has no finite value. Reverse extent is nevertheless feasible: x lies in[−2,0]. At x=−1 the composition is(1,1,1), which preserves both component totals and has Q=K=1.
items.transfer: In the different mixture(2,0,0), is reverse conversion available? Use the feasible interval instead of assigning a value to0/0.

items.prompt: An ideal A + B ⇌ C mixture is initially at(1,1,1) with K=1. Add A at fixed volume so that, before any conversion, its new composition is(2,1,1). Which statement is correct at that instant?
options: Q=2, so net reverse conversion is favored.
Q=1 and all concentrations are still at equilibrium.
K changes to1/2 while Q stays1.
Q=1/2 while K stays1, so net forward conversion is favored.
items.explanation: Immediately after the addition, Q=1/(2×1)=1/2. K stays1 under the stated constant-temperature model. Forward conversion lowers A and B and raises C until the changed component totals admit a new equilibrium.
items.transfer: Instead remove C from the original(1,1,1) mixture to make(1,1,0). Calculate the immediate Q and predict the net direction without asserting complete conversion.

items.prompt: A reversible reaction has a large equilibrium constant at a specified temperature. Which statement correctly separates equilibrium information from kinetics?
options: A large K guarantees completion within one second.
K alone gives the time needed to reach equilibrium.
K alone does not supply a reaction timescale.
A large K proves that no reactants can remain at equilibrium.
items.explanation: K constrains equilibrium composition together with the starting component totals. It supplies no rate constants or timescale. A large positive finite K also does not, by itself, justify declaring every reactant concentration exactly zero.
items.transfer: Name one additional kind of information needed to predict composition as a function of time.

items.prompt: For ideal A + B ⇌ C, start from(a,b,c)=(2,0,0), with positive finite K. Which report respects both nonnegative concentrations and the quotient's domain?
options: Only x=0 is feasible; Q is undefined because its denominator is zero.
Q=0 and a positive forward extent is feasible.
Q=K because both numerator and denominator of Q are zero.
A negative extent can consume C even though none is present.
items.explanation: The feasible interval is[−c,min(a,b)]=[0,0], so no conversion is available. Q=0/(2×0) is undefined. The model should report no feasible change without fabricating a finite quotient or saying that undefined Q equals K.
items.transfer: Compare this mixture with(2,0,1). Explain why adding C changes the feasible directions even though B still starts at zero.

items.prompt: An exact-arithmetic solver brackets the root of a continuous strictly decreasing equilibrium residual with f(lo)≥0 and f(hi)≤0. The bracket has nonzero width. Which interpretation is justified?
options: The displayed midpoint is the exact physical root, regardless of rounding.
The root lies in the bracket; its midpoint is an estimate, and the bracket describes numerical refinement.
The bracket is automatically an experimental confidence interval.
Each refinement step equals one second of reaction time.
items.explanation: Continuity gives a root between the sign-bounding endpoints, and strict decrease makes that root unique. A nonzero-width bracket does not turn a midpoint into an exact root. Its width describes this calculation, not measurement variation or reaction time.
items.transfer: What would a zero-width bracket with exact residual zero justify? Name one real-system limitation it would still not remove.
